title: Church bells, steamboats, the Italian brass band and grandmother's riverfront lunches
summary: He describes the church bells, steamboat whistles and the big Italian brass band, then how his grandmother fed the riverfront gangs and whether there was music there.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

the steamboats the river boats I hear these long drawn out steamboat blasts arrivals and departures of boats and all kind of weird whistles from those river packets also there was river packets and like I said you heard all kind of folks singing and they were with gypsies they were singing their music and the most outstanding thing I remember was this big Italian brass concert band it used to march from the Sunless Pathoges to St. Mary's Church and those lines and and charlis during the summer every Sunday there was some sort of Italian or French procession Catholic religious procession and had this great big brass band sometimes as many as a hundred pieces which also included a lot of small kids in the uniform that the grown-ups wear and they had beautiful marches and they marched slow down down Charles Street from the Sunless Church or they marched further down to other churches up uptown to the St. Patrick's Church which is probably where they were all first-rate musicians in a brass band sense I imagine and followed they had all the brass instruments and later on when I got to realize it was happening to my grandfather and the Arnold brass band and I wondered how just about nine or ten men could get so much music after and I got to and I got to and I got to and I got to and I got to and I got to and I got to and I got to and I got to and I got to and I got to and I got to and I had to and I had to She was called a moshon lady, a merchant. She used to fix food for the Whitmans and the gangs. They had 14, 15 members of a gang. Sometimes she'd take over two gangs and feed them hot food. And she'd put on these big pots of food, red beans and rice, cabbage and rice, stew and rice. She'd make a big pudding. She'd make cupcakes, cornbread, hot biscuits. And me and my young aunts, my young cousins, would help her with these three or four big baskets of food. And around 11, 1130 we'd leave for the river, which was a few blocks away, three or four blocks, short blocks. Sometimes half a dozen blocks, we'd walk out to the river, just in time as the whistle would blow for the gangs to break. And we'd walk out on the river front up on the wall. And she always knew my grandfather's gang was Wiccans. And we'd find a big old crate or something that they were cotton bales or anything they were handling and shipping. And place all the stuff on top and she'd take out these napkins, put these buckets out. The buckets would prepare as individual lunches, like rice and red beans, whatever it was. Give them a bucket and a knife in the fork. And it was a hot meal, which they needed them other than the sandwich to fight that hard and have their work out on the river. As long as they were loading the ships in time, three or four days, maybe seven days, two and Sundays, she'd bring these meals out there. Did they have any music on the river then? No, I never saw no music on the river. Only on paid there, like on a Friday or Saturday, the blind men would come up and sing for the awake moments as they would gather around the pay office to get paid. And sometimes they'd have some preachers there, a preacher made a couple of sisters, a missionary away from the church. They'd come out there and sing and preach a while.
